title: Controversial Film Opinion: Modern Cinema Outshines Classics

commenti.body:
I'm always sceptical towards the attitude that filmmaking is spiralling down into a cesspit of mediocrity. There is a nostalgic reflection upon the past which unconsciously omits the plenitude of bad films that would be been being made then. People like to remember and single out only what they consider to be the best, and then they attribute the quality of these examples to the epoch as a whole.

There have been some tremendous films in the past year. Dance First, Anatomy of a Fall, All of us Strangers and Oppenheimer. In the past 20, countless. In 2018, we had The House That Jack Built. Perhaps I'm in the minority, but I consider it one of the greatest films ever made. There are innumerable examples of modern cinema which would show that it is anything but brilliant. Just because the reactionary, grifting 'critics' of youtube would have people believe that film is in same sort of crisis, because they aren't getting masterful kino from blockbusters and marvel dross, that doesn't mean that we haven't received and won't continue to receive excellent films.

I don't know that I would say that modern cinema necessarily 'outshines' classics. I'm not sure that I've seen anything that has affected me more than a Salo, or a Barry Lyndon, or a Fire Walk With Me. But there is nothing to suggest to me that we are in some period of tragic decline, either.

You've watched a handful of English-language movies made over the span of \~75 years, decided they are representative of the entire history of cinema, and then concluded that this entire era of film is inferior to the past few years? And you think this is an intellectually defensible argument?

I think mainstream cinema is largely a cesspit of mediocrity. Of course there are exceptions, and of course there has always been plenty of mediocre films to go around. 

I also totally agree with the last point you made. I watched Dr. Strangelove for the first time a week ago and wow it was amazing. I can think of few modern films that even begin to approach that level of quality and artistry (although therw are definitely some). I may not enjoy all the classics but as I have been working my way thru them their are certainly many of great quality and quite a few that are even mind-blowingly good and I struggle to think of much of anything that could compare. Another example is the film Koyaanisqatsi, which I also watched recently. A fantastic and interesting movie, and I feel like there is a lack of quality films that are so good and yet so experimental and abstract.

I always have a hard time comparing cinematic eras in this sort of way, using words like “outshine” and discussing differences in “quality.” I find it useful to remember that films exist in the context of their time and that often shows up in the film’s aesthetics, storytelling conventions, acting, etc. Things sure do look, sound, and feel a lot different today than they did in 1950. Our preferences are so often shaped by the media around us. We like what we’re used to. It’s easy to consume, easy to understand.

While your preference for modern cinema is certainly valid, I think it might fun to ask yourself “why?” more often. Not to second guess the things you enjoy, but to better understand your own assumptions. Why are subtlety and complexity synonymous with “genuine human experiences” in your mind? Why is nuance a more effective artistic choice than simplicity? Why did a particular classic filmmaker make the choices he or she made? Maybe you end up with the same answers you’ve already reached for yourself. That’s fine. But I can’t shake the feeling that you’re missing out on the richness of different forms of filmmaking and storytelling that I think are as impactful as the greatest examples of today.

In the case of The Seventh Seal (and a lot of Bergman tbh), it’s the simplicity that does it for me. When I hear the characters wonder aloud, in a straightforward manner, as they wrestle with our most relatable existential questions - it floors me. It’s almost shocking to hear Antonius speak so frankly. And, as for the acting style, it might also help to understand Bergman as a director of the Swedish theater. 

I feel like I’m rambling without a coherent point but I guess I think your opinions are fine but think you should keep seeking!

I think there are still very good films coming out but there's also such a massive volume of garbage that the ratio appears to be much much worse. There's also an overly polished feel to current films now that to me removes a lot of the life from them. There's also the fact that the further you go through time the harder it will be to make something that is doing something new.


That being said. I do find on average films in the past seem to take on themes that seemed far more profound for the human condition. I don't know if this is largely because in the few decades following the second world our civilization had to contend with all the downstream consequences of that, the Holocaust, living through the cold war and vietnam. Religion was more prominent so more traditional religious themes played more heavily into art. Spielberg was influenced heavily by his father being a ww2 vet, he was very focused on that time period, and being a Jew he needed to contend with the Holocaust. We can look at scorsese, who's quite religious and neurotic and that shows up in his work and the way he explores human morality. 


I think a lot of the modern films I like seem to literally be made by the same people who were making films during the golden age in the 70s, or in the 90s which was also another great time. I think a lot of modern films have kind of a terrible mix of a sort of post modern view of the human condition, where they seem to have abandoned all conventional knowledge and are trying to reinvent the human from scratch, which just doesn't land with me because it's alienating more than anything. And then a horrible sort of hyper progressiveness that is so transparent and propagandistic that it's really impossible to call the manipulative swill they are making art. The extreme political correctness and identity politics that pervades so many modern films has absolutely stripped them of any useful insights or anything intriguing.


I think Tarantino is right that films come in waves and right now we are probably in the worst wave yet. In the 80s the films were definitely worse overall than the 70s and 90s, but it still had some great films overall. Same as now, we still have some fantastic films coming out, but as a percentage of everything currently being made it's not great.


I do have hope that things will begin to turn around, and maybe this year may be that turning point and we will start to enter another decade of amazing films.

Oh I am not a fan of this take at all. 

I will say that I think film, as a technical medium, generally gets better as time goes on. The average person has reasonable access to equipment that would make someone like Hitchcock or Kurosawa or Dreyer jealous. The professionals have access to equipment that the directors of old couldn't even fathom in their wildest dreams. 

Art also tends to build upon itself. Let's take Man with a Movie Camera. This movie wouldn't even get a passing grade in film school today. But when it was released, it was absolutely revolutionary. What is released today is going to be expanded upon, from a technical perspective, by movies released 5, 10, 25, 50 years from now. 

But I do not buy the fact that movies of today are somehow more compelling than movies of the past. I have watched 204 of the 264 movies that made Sight and Sound's 2022 list. I have watched 1500 movies in the last two years, and god knows how many movies I have watched before I started keeping track. I mean, I am pushing 40. I have seen a lot of movies. 

I have seen movies of today that absolutely blew me away. Last year was such a wonderful year for movies. But I absolutely would put the very best movies from 50+ years ago against the best movies of today. 

One of the things that I did when I started watching movies of the past, I try to familiarize myself with that world. Maybe part of the problem is a lack of context? One of my favorite African films is Black Girl. It was made in 1966 and was a coproduction of Senegal and France. Understanding the colonial attitudes of France in the 1960s is important. I mean, Senegal just got their independence from France less than a decade before the release of the movie. Understanding the historical and culture context of this time and place really helped put this movie into perspective. I mean, it would have been just a pretty good movie without it, but with a little bit of understanding of that time and place really elevated the film.

Those are all pretty standard Hollywood affairs. Today, we have that plus Terrence Malick, PTA, Lucretia Martel, Park Chan-wook, Lee Chang-dong, Thomas Vinterberg, Weerasethakul, Sciamma, Reygadas, Sono and many more.
every one of these films are action adventure films or musical comedies, barring one which is a music biopic. I don't disagree with your thesis but these are bad examples.

I always take it with a grain of salt when ppl make grand, sweeping statements like this.

The classics are classics because of many factors, but most importantly, it’s time. It’s also the fact that ppl still analyze, watch, rewatch, discover, discuss and be amazed by them over and over again despite coming out say 90 years ago. There’s a sense of timelessness to them. City Lights still brings audiences to tears despite premiering over 9 decades ago. Today’s films stand on the shoulders of giants that like changed the game.

To be frank, I’m not sure if we’ll be talking about Columbus in 50 years lol 

I think the real discussion in all this is the dilution of the medium due to its treatment as less an art form and more as content.

tl;dr It’s impossible to conclusively state this unless you can travel to the future.

I agree completely about mainstream cinema. There are a few gems here and there, but for the most part, it's utter dross. That said, there are some wonderful films outside the mainstream, that being where you find the real quality. I think the only truly substantial difference between new and old is that with the general commercialisation of everything, the ever-evolving mechanics of capitalism, and the gradu decrease in attention-span and demand for quality, it has become more difficult to pierce the veil of mediocrity and uncover these gems.

I don't have much to add to this conversation except to say that I'm of a similar mindset; I'm just not bold enough to risk sharing the unpopular opinion! I keep telling myself that maybe I haven't watched enough classic cinema (and I haven't!) but with each film I do watch, I feel a bit more validated.

Definitely agree on Seventh Seal. The premise sounded great, but ultimately I was disappointed for the reasons you stated and have been slow to check out more Bergman since.

I will say though that Lawrence of Arabia is the kind of classic film that *does* live up to the hype for me. It's hard to imagine an epic film that's basically a character study being made today.

I’m not sure a person who “rarely watch[es] non-English movies because it’s difficult to read subtitles” is in a position to assert the superiority of classic Hollywood and chastise others for knocking films they haven’t seen. I’m not agreeing or disagreeing, just suggesting that  a curious mind and a bit of humility can open up a lot of doors.
